Any two of the characteristics listed in section 13.2.2. (1) EM waves are transverse: the electric field \( \vec{E} \), the magnetic field \( \vec{B} \) and the direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular, and the two fields vary sinusoidally in phase with each other. (2) EM waves need no material medium; in free space they all travel with the same speed \( c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}} = 3 \times 10^{8} \) m/s. (Other acceptable pairs: they are produced by accelerated charges; the ratio of the field amplitudes is constant at every point, \( |E_{0}|/|B_{0}| = c \); they obey the principle of superposition; their energy is shared equally between the electric and the magnetic field.)
Two characteristics: EM waves are transverse with \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, and they propagate through free space with speed \( 3 \times 10^{8} \) m/s.

Radar locates distant objects such as ships and aeroplanes by sending out a beam and timing the echo reflected from the target, and microwaves suit that job for three reasons. Their wavelength is short (about \( 3 \times 10^{-4} \) m to \( 6 \times 10^{-2} \) m), so they can be sent out as a narrow, highly directional beam that travels in a straight line and can resolve a small object instead of spreading in all directions. Their frequency is far above 30 MHz, so they are not turned back by the ionosphere but pass straight through it to the target. And being of such short wavelength they are strongly reflected by metallic bodies, so a measurable echo returns from the object.
Microwaves are used in radar because their short wavelength gives a narrow, straight, highly directional beam that is strongly reflected by distant metallic objects.

EM waves are waves caused by the acceleration of charged particles, consisting of an electric field and a magnetic field vibrating sinusoidally at right angles to each other and to the direction of propagation. They are periodic changes in the electric and magnetic fields that propagate through space and transport energy, needing no material medium to travel; in free space every one of them moves with the speed of light, \( c = 3 \times 10^{8} \) m/s.
EM waves are transverse waves of mutually perpendicular, in-phase oscillating electric and magnetic fields, produced by accelerated charges and able to travel through free space.

By Maxwell's theory, accelerated charges radiate EM waves. A charge oscillating with some frequency sets up an oscillating electric field in the space around it; by the Ampere-Maxwell law that changing electric field produces an oscillating magnetic field, and by Faraday's law the changing magnetic field in turn produces an electric field. The two fields thus regenerate each other and the disturbance travels outwards as an EM wave of the same frequency as the oscillation of the charge. A charge at rest has only a static electric field and radiates nothing, and a charge in uniform motion gives a magnetic field that does not change with time, so it too radiates nothing; acceleration is essential. In practice this is done by an oscillator circuit containing an inductor and a capacitor (radio waves and microwaves), by fast electrons striking a high atomic number target (X-rays), by transitions of orbital electrons between energy levels (visible light and ultraviolet), and by transitions of nuclear energy levels (gamma rays).
EM waves are produced by accelerated (in particular, oscillating) electric charges.

No, a purely electric or a purely magnetic wave cannot be produced in space. A time varying magnetic field induces an electric field (Faraday's law), and a time varying electric field produces a magnetic field through the displacement current term (the Ampere-Maxwell law). So the moment either field varies with time it creates the other, and the two regenerate each other as the disturbance travels. Neither field can propagate on its own.
No, because a changing electric field always produces a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field always produces an electric field, so the two must occur together in any EM wave.

Yes. The filament of an ordinary electric lamp is at a high temperature, so it radiates visible light, and being a hot body it radiates a great deal of infrared as well. Both visible light and infrared are EM waves, and section 13.1 names light bulbs among the everyday sources of EM waves.
Yes, an ordinary electric lamp emits EM waves, mainly visible light and infrared radiation.

Light is an EM wave. It consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that regenerate each other, and such fields can exist in empty space, so light needs no matter to carry it and travels through vacuum with speed \( 3 \times 10^{8} \) m/s. Sound is a mechanical wave: it is carried forward by the to-and-fro motion of the particles of a material medium, each layer passing the disturbance to the next. A vacuum has no particles to oscillate and no elasticity to transmit the compressions and rarefactions, so sound cannot travel through it.
Light travels in vacuum because it is an EM wave of electric and magnetic fields needing no medium, whereas sound is a mechanical wave that needs the particles of a material medium.

Ultraviolet rays are EM waves lying just beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum, with wavelengths of about \( 3 \times 10^{-8} \) m to \( 4 \times 10^{-7} \) m (frequencies \( 8 \times 10^{14} \) Hz to \( 1 \times 10^{16} \) Hz). They are produced by the rearrangement of the orbital electrons of atoms between energy levels, as in a mercury vapour lamp, an electric spark, a carbon arc lamp, or an electrical discharge in hydrogen or xenon. The Sun is the most important natural source, and most of its ultraviolet is absorbed by the ozone layer of the Earth's atmosphere. They produce fluorescence in materials such as phosphors, cause the photoelectric effect, are stopped by glass but pass through quartz, and help the skin synthesise vitamin D.
Two uses: (1) they destroy germs and bacteria, so they are used for sterilizing surgical instruments and for purification of water; (2) they are used to detect forgery, and likewise to distinguish real gems from fake ones.

Radio waves are the longest wavelength EM waves. They are produced by the accelerated motion of charges in a conducting wire, in practice by an oscillator circuit whose inductance and capacitance are chosen to fix the frequency required. Their wavelengths range from a few centimetres to a few hundred kilometres. The AM band runs from 530 kHz to 1710 kHz, TV transmission from 54 MHz to 890 MHz, and the FM radio band from 88 MHz to 108 MHz.
Two uses: (1) radio broadcasting and the transmission of TV signals; (2) wireless communication generally, for example cellular phones, which carry voice communication in the ultra high frequency (UHF) band.

Ultraviolet rays. They are an ionizing radiation, and an overdose kills or damages living plant and animal tissue. The Sun is their most important natural source, and although most of the incoming ultraviolet is absorbed by the ozone layer, a significant part still reaches the lower atmosphere and the ground. Gamma rays and X-rays are of higher energy still, but radiation of those kinds arriving from space is absorbed almost completely by the atmospheric gases and dust high above us, so it is the ultraviolet that actually gets through and does the harm.
The most harmful radiation entering the Earth's atmosphere from outer space is ultraviolet radiation.

(i) The short wave band lies between 3 MHz and 30 MHz, which is the sky wave range. Waves of these frequencies are reflected back to the Earth by the ionosphere and can suffer repeated reflections between the ionosphere and the ground, so a single transmitter reaches receivers thousands of kilometres away. Waves below about 2 MHz travel as ground waves, induce currents in the ground and lose their energy by absorption, so they serve local broadcasting only; and waves above 30 MHz pass through the ionosphere instead of returning. Hence long distance radio broadcast uses the short wave band.
(ii) TV signals occupy 54 MHz to 890 MHz, well above 30 MHz, so the ionosphere does not reflect them back and sky wave propagation is not available. They must travel as space (line of sight) waves, whose range is limited by the curvature of the Earth to \( d \approx \sqrt{2Rh} \); even a 600 m tower reaches under 90 km. A satellite acts as an extremely tall relay station: it receives the signal from the ground transmitter and retransmits it, so one satellite can cover a whole continent. Hence satellites are used for long distance TV transmission.

Every communication system has three basic elements: the transmitter, which converts the information into a form suitable for sending through the channel; the communication channel, the passage (wires, cables or a wireless link) through which the signal travels; and the receiver, which picks the signal up at the far end of the channel and reconstructs the original message for the user.
The three basic units are the transmitter, the communication channel and the receiver.

A carrier wave is a high frequency wave on which a low frequency information signal is superimposed so that the signal can be transmitted over a large distance. One of the characteristics of the carrier, its amplitude, its frequency or its phase, is varied in accordance with the amplitude of the signal, which is the process of modulation; the carrier itself carries no information and merely carries the signal.
A carrier wave is the high frequency wave used to carry a low frequency message signal, one of whose properties is varied in step with the signal during modulation.

An audio signal is of low frequency, below about 20 kHz, and cannot be radiated over a large distance as it is. For efficient transmission an antenna must be at least \( \lambda/4 \) long, and for a 15 kHz audio signal that works out to about 5 km, which is impracticable; a high frequency carrier has a wavelength of only a few metres, so an antenna of ordinary size will do. The power radiated by an antenna also falls off steeply as the wavelength grows, so a low frequency wave radiates feebly and dies out quickly, whereas a high frequency wave radiates efficiently and travels far. Finally, if every station transmitted its audio directly, all the transmissions would lie in the same narrow band and would get mixed up, while different carrier frequencies can be allotted to different transmitters.
High frequency carrier waves are used because they allow an antenna of practical size, radiate power efficiently over long distances, and let each transmitter be separated from the others by its own frequency.

Modulation is the process of superimposing a low frequency information signal on a high frequency carrier wave by varying one of the characteristics of the carrier, its amplitude, its frequency or its phase, in proportion to the amplitude of the signal, the other two properties being kept unchanged. It is carried out at the transmitter and is what makes it possible to send a low frequency signal over a large distance; it also keeps the transmissions of different stations from mixing, since each can be given its own carrier frequency.
Modulation is the superimposing of a low frequency signal on a high frequency carrier wave by varying the amplitude, frequency or phase of the carrier in accordance with the signal.

Amplitude modulation is the type of modulation in which the amplitude of the carrier wave is varied in accordance with the amplitude (intensity) of the signal wave, the frequency and the phase of the carrier being kept constant. The outline traced by the peaks of the modulated wave then reproduces the shape of the signal. Amplitude modulation is simple to implement, cheap and has a large range, but it is not efficient in its use of power and it is prone to noise, so the reproduced signal may not exactly match the original; it is used for commercial broadcasting in the long, medium and short wave bands.
Amplitude modulation is modulation in which only the amplitude of the carrier wave is varied in proportion to the amplitude of the signal.

Noise is a random unwanted signal that mixes with the message signal in a communication system and distorts it. The source that generates the noise may lie inside the system, for instance in its own electronic circuits, or outside it, for instance lightning or the sparking of electrical machinery. Since noise degrades the received message, every effort is made to keep the noise level in a communication system as low as possible.
Noise is a random unwanted signal that interferes with the message signal in a communication system.

The bandwidth of an electronic circuit is the range of frequencies over which it operates efficiently, that is, the difference between the highest and the lowest frequency it can handle without appreciable loss. The same idea applies to a communication channel, and a message can be transmitted faithfully only if the bandwidth available is at least as wide as the band of frequencies that the signal occupies.
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies over which a circuit or a channel works efficiently.

Demodulation is the process of regaining the original low frequency message signal from the modulated carrier wave that arrives at the receiver. It is the reverse of modulation: modulation is done at the transmitter, demodulation at the receiver, and it is what recovers the speech, music or picture that the carrier was carrying.
Demodulation is the recovery of the original signal from a modulated wave, the reverse of modulation.

A television broadcast carries two signals together, and the two are modulated differently. The picture (video) signal is transmitted by amplitude modulation, and the accompanying sound (audio) signal is transmitted by frequency modulation. Frequency modulation is chosen for the sound because it reproduces the original signal closely and is much less susceptible to noise, which is what a listener notices at once; amplitude modulation is used for the video signal because it keeps the bandwidth needed and the receiver circuitry manageable. (This chapter states the properties of amplitude and of frequency modulation but does not itself say which is used for television; the pairing above is the standard practice.)
Television broadcast uses amplitude modulation for the picture signal and frequency modulation for the sound signal.

For a linear antenna of a given length \( l \), the effective power radiated is proportional to \( (l/\lambda)^{2} \), so for a fixed antenna length the radiated power varies inversely as the square of the wavelength. The power therefore falls off very rapidly as the wavelength is increased: a long wavelength (low frequency) signal radiates very feebly, while shortening the wavelength raises the radiated power sharply. This is one of the reasons a low frequency audio signal is put on a short wavelength, high frequency carrier before it is transmitted. (This chapter does not print the relation itself; it is consistent with the statement in the chapter that an antenna must be at least \( \lambda/4 \) long for efficient transmission and reception.)
Effective power radiated \( \propto 1/\lambda^{2} \).

All transmitters radiate into the same space, so their waves arrive together at every receiving antenna. If two broadcasting stations used the same carrier frequency their programmes would get mixed up and no tuning circuit could separate them, because a receiver selects a station by responding to its frequency. Allotting a different carrier frequency to each transmitter keeps the stations in separate bands, so a receiver tuned to one frequency picks up that programme alone and the others do not interfere with it.
Different frequencies are used so that the signals of different transmitters do not get mixed up and a receiver can select any one station by tuning to its frequency.

A message signal such as speech or music is a low frequency signal, below about 20 kHz, and it cannot be transmitted over a large distance on its own for three reasons. First, an antenna must be at least \( \lambda/4 \) long to transmit and receive efficiently, and for a 15 kHz audio signal that is about 5 km, which cannot be built. Second, the power radiated by an antenna falls off steeply as the wavelength increases, so at audio wavelengths hardly any energy is radiated and the signal does not travel. Third, all transmitters would be radiating in the same low band, so the programmes of different stations would overlap and could not be separated. Superimposing the message on a high frequency carrier removes all three limitations at once: the wavelength becomes short enough for an antenna of ordinary size, the wave radiates efficiently and travels far, and each transmitter can be given a carrier frequency of its own.
A carrier wave is necessary because it makes a low frequency signal radiable by an antenna of practical size, gives it the range to travel long distances, and keeps the transmissions of different stations separable.

In amplitude modulation the whole of the information is carried by the variation in the amplitude of the carrier wave. Most of the noise a wave picks up on its way, from lightning, from the sparking of electrical machinery and from the circuits themselves, is also a random variation of amplitude, so it adds directly to the amplitude pattern that carries the message. The receiver recovers the signal by following that pattern, and it has no way of telling the wanted amplitude variation from the unwanted one, so the noise is reproduced along with the programme and the signal that comes out may not exactly match the original. Frequency modulation does not suffer in this way, because there the information lies in the frequency and not in the amplitude, which is why frequency modulation is used for high quality broadcast transmission.
Amplitude modulation gives noisy reception because the message is carried by the amplitude of the wave, and noise is itself an amplitude variation that the receiver cannot separate from the signal.

The signals to be sent in a communication system, speech and music for instance, are low frequency signals, and a low frequency signal cannot be transmitted over a large distance as it stands. Modulation superimposes it on a high frequency carrier wave and thereby solves three separate problems. (1) Antenna size: an antenna must be at least \( \lambda/4 \) long for efficient transmission, which is about 5 km for a 15 kHz audio signal but only a few metres for a carrier of a few MHz. (2) Radiated power and range: the power radiated by an antenna falls off steeply with increasing wavelength, so a low frequency wave radiates feebly and does not travel far, while a high frequency carrier radiates efficiently. (3) Mixing of stations: different carrier frequencies can be allotted to different transmitters, so their signals do not get mixed up and a receiver can select any one of them.
Modulation is needed to make a low frequency signal transmissible over long distances with an antenna of practical size, and to keep the transmissions of different stations separate.

For any EM wave \( c = \nu\lambda \), so \( \nu = c/\lambda \).
Here \( \lambda = 250 \) m and \( c = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \) m/s.
\( \nu = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{250} = 1.2 \times 10^{6} \) Hz.
Since 1 MHz \( = 10^{6} \) Hz, the frequency of the radio wave is 1.2 MHz.

For any EM wave \( c = \nu\lambda \), so \( \lambda = c/\nu \).
Here \( \nu = 2.0 \times 10^{18} \) Hz and \( c = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \) m/s.
\( \lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.0 \times 10^{18}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-10} \) m.
Since 1 nm \( = 10^{-9} \) m, the wavelength of the X-ray is 0.15 nm (that is, \( 1.5 \) angstrom).

[Textbook note: the printed answer \(4.6 \times 10^{14}\) Hz is the value above rounded to two significant figures; the stem's data give \(4.62 \times 10^{14}\) Hz.]

For any EM wave \( c = \nu\lambda \), so \( \nu = c/\lambda \).
Here \( \lambda = 6.5 \times 10^{-7} \) m and \( c = 3 \times 10^{8} \) m/s.
\( \nu = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{6.5 \times 10^{-7}} = 0.4615 \times 10^{15} \) Hz.
The frequency of the red light is \( 4.62 \times 10^{14} \) Hz.

For any EM wave \( c = \nu\lambda \), so \( \lambda = c/\nu \).
Here \( \nu = 8.0 \) GHz \( = 8.0 \times 10^{9} \) Hz and \( c = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \) m/s.
\( \lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{8.0 \times 10^{9}} = 3.75 \times 10^{-2} \) m.
The wavelength of the microwave is \( 3.75 \times 10^{-2} \) m, that is 3.75 cm.

u = 2 	imes 10^{10} \) Hz. Using \( c = 
u\lambda \),
\( \lambda = \dfrac{c}{
u} = \dfrac{3 	imes 10^{8}}{2 	imes 10^{10}} = 1.5 	imes 10^{-2} \) m.
The wavelength of the wave is \( 1.5 	imes 10^{-2} \) m, that is 1.5 cm.

In an EM wave the ratio of the amplitudes of the electric and the magnetic field is constant at every point and equals the speed of the wave (equation 13.1): \( |E_{0}| = c\,|B_{0}| \).
Here \( B_{0} = 5 \times 10^{-7} \) T and \( c = 3 \times 10^{8} \) m/s.
\( E_{0} = (3 \times 10^{8})(5 \times 10^{-7}) = 150 \) V/m.
The amplitude of the electric field is 150 V/m, that is \( 1.5 \times 10^{2} \) V/m.

The signal travels as a space wave, so its range is \( d = \sqrt{2Rh} \).
Here \( h = 200 \) m and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^{6} \) m, so
\( d = \sqrt{2 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6} \times 200} = \sqrt{2.56 \times 10^{9}} = 5.06 \times 10^{4} \) m \( = 50.6 \) km.
The area covered is a circle of this radius, and since \( d^{2} = 2Rh = 2.56 \times 10^{9} \) m\( ^{2} = 2.56 \times 10^{3} \) km\( ^{2} \),
area \( = \pi d^{2} = 3.14 \times 2.56 \times 10^{3} = 8.04 \times 10^{3} \) km\( ^{2} \).
Population covered \( = \) area \( \times \) population density \( = (8.04 \times 10^{3})(1000) \).
The transmission covers about \( 8.0 \times 10^{6} \) people, that is roughly 80 lakh.

The coverage range of a space wave is \( d = \sqrt{2Rh} \).
Here \( h = 600 \) m and \( R = 6400 \) km \( = 6.4 \times 10^{6} \) m, so
\( d = \sqrt{2 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6} \times 600} = \sqrt{7.68 \times 10^{9}} = 8.76 \times 10^{4} \) m \( = 87.6 \) km.
For the second part, the coverage area is \( A = \pi d^{2} = \pi (2Rh) \), which is directly proportional to the height \( h \). Doubling the area therefore needs the height to be doubled, not the range:
\( h' = 2h = 2 \times 600 = 1200 \) m. (Check: \( d' = \sqrt{2 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6} \times 1200} = 123.9 \) km, and \( (123.9/87.6)^{2} = 2 \).)
The coverage range is about 87.6 km, and a height of 1200 m is needed to double the coverage area.

When both the transmitting and the receiving antenna are raised, the line of sight range is the sum of the two individual ranges:
\( d_{max} = \sqrt{2Rh_{t}} + \sqrt{2Rh_{r}} \).
Here \( h_{t} = 32 \) m, \( h_{r} = 50 \) m and \( R = 6.4 \times 10^{6} \) m.
\( \sqrt{2Rh_{t}} = \sqrt{2 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6} \times 32} = \sqrt{4.096 \times 10^{8}} = 2.02 \times 10^{4} \) m \( = 20.2 \) km.
\( \sqrt{2Rh_{r}} = \sqrt{2 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6} \times 50} = \sqrt{6.4 \times 10^{8}} = 2.53 \times 10^{4} \) m \( = 25.3 \) km.
\( d_{max} = 20.2 + 25.3 = 45.5 \) km.
The maximum distance for satisfactory line of sight communication is about \( 4.55 \times 10^{4} \) m, that is 45.5 km.
